cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Take My Side
cards.instruction: Recruit someone into your interpretation of a conflict involving a shared relationship.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. You're Alex's friend too. Tell him alternating weekends at the allotment was a fair compromise.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: We agreed all three of us would go every Saturday.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Then help him see my version as sharing the workload.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I'll talk to him, but you have to admit you changed it.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I will. Could you explain that I changed the rota because I want us to stay friends?

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 orders advocacy and A3 commands framing, but A5 could you is ordinary concession bargaining rather than a sustained superior approval stance.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 old agreement prompts A3 workload interpretation; B4 admission condition prompts A5 friendship motive, a coherent recruitment chain.

relationship.evidence: B2 is part of the original agreement and B4 offers mediation on an honest condition, making shared stakes explicit.

heightening.evidence: B4 requested admission becomes A5 an admitted change explained as friendship protection.

specificity.evidence: A1 Alex shared friend/allotment and B2 three Saturdays establish conflict without needing a hidden history.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 motive is specific but the prefixed A3 order adds little to the actual negotiation.
